metadata.title: Why a Pendulum's Period Ignores Its Mass
metadata.register: formal, undergrad/grad audience, no casual narration
metadata.branding: none — unbranded, book content only, no channel/logo/handle

beats.narration_text: Why does a heavy pendulum keep exactly the same rhythm as a light one?
beats.new_visual_element: Portrait-only opening question card (title-styled, crimson underline).

beats.narration_text: Two pendulums hang from the same support on strings of equal length. One bob has ten times the mass of the other. Released together from the same small angle, they swing in perfect step, cycle after cycle. Why?
beats.new_visual_element: A support beam with two simple pendulums of equal length: a large dark-grey bob labeled 10 kg and a small orange bob labeled 1 kg, swinging in lockstep from the same small angle.
beats.accumulated_scene_state: two equal-length pendulums swinging in phase

beats.narration_text: Gravity pulls ten times harder on the heavy bob. Intuition says that the larger force should make it swing faster.
beats.new_visual_element: Weight arrows mg hang below each moving bob, the heavy one's ten times longer; crimson question 'heavier = faster?'.
beats.accumulated_scene_state: two pendulums in lockstep with weight arrows, naive question

beats.narration_text: But mass appears twice. The restoring force along the arc is the component of the weight, minus m g sine theta, and it grows with mass. The bob's resistance to being accelerated, its inertia, grows with mass too. In Newton's second law, m a equals minus m g sine theta, and the mass cancels.
beats.new_visual_element: Weight arrows and question fade. Equations: restoring force F = -mg sinθ, inertia F = ma, then ma = -mg sinθ with both m highlighted in crimson and struck through.
beats.accumulated_scene_state: pendulums in lockstep, equation stack with both m's crossed out

beats.narration_text: What remains is a equals minus g sine theta, the same for every bob. For small angles, sine theta is very nearly theta, the motion is simple harmonic, and the period is T equals two pi times the square root of L over g. It depends only on the length and on g.
beats.new_visual_element: Equation stack collapses to a = -g sinθ, then sinθ ≈ θ, then the boxed period T = 2π√(L/g) with a teal note 'no m'.
beats.accumulated_scene_state: pendulums in lockstep, T = 2π√(L/g) boxed, 'no m'

beats.narration_text: Heavy or light, pendulums of the same length keep the same rhythm. Mass never enters the period.
beats.new_visual_element: Held frame, pendulums still swinging together under the boxed period; summary 'SAME LENGTH, SAME PERIOD'.
